title: Why Jensen Huang proved too big to fire
description: There have been three jaw-dropping moments in the past few hours around Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief executive after he admitted an af
body: There have been three jaw-dropping moments in the past few hours around Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief executive after he admitted an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy.The shock announcement of his return to the chipmaker was followed by the addition of one trillion dollars of stock market value to Nvidia.Then it was the moment President Trump admitted the obvious: that it was his "You're unfired" message direct to the board that changed the decision.The nature of the U-turn is clear from what Nvidia was saying just last week. The board was clear that Huang was not returning. The interim management had also suggested some shifts in strategy away from the Huang era.All of that is now in the dustbin of corporate history. This is a comeback that exceeds the return of Sam Altman to OpenAI or Steve Jobs to Apple, in terms of sheer numbers.LIVE: Nvidia shares soar after Jensen Huang returns as CEOThe rise and fall and rise again of Jensen HuangHow important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?The reason for the turnaround was pretty clear in the first statement. The US government had said there were no national security concerns with his reinstatement. Such a reassurance could only have come from the White House.And an hour later President Trump revealed that he had spoken directly to the Nvidia board.This is where I go back to my own conversation with Jensen Huang last September, where he openly advocated for allowing Chinese access to advanced Nvidia microchips. He was one of the few people in the world who could credibly say he knew the minds of both President Trump and President Xi.Reports in the US say there were splits in the Trump administration between China hawks wanting to restrict exports, and others who backed Huang's argument. There is still an independent investigation into the company's compliance with export controls.Nvidia's chips are critical to the development of frontier artificial intelligence systems. Jensen Huang's influence over this pipeline meant he was more important than many world leaders.This is a move of importance not just to the flagging US tech stock boom, but the future of the world economy, of US politics, and of course the geopolitical race between the US and China.The recent doubts about Nvidia struck at the heart of the AI boom. This is after all a company actually generating phenomenal amounts of real sales - over $400bn (£305bn) this year, compared with $27bn four years ago.Nvidia's stock market valuation has been used as a critical form of financing for other companies to construct data centres. A complex web of loans, guarantees, and shareholdings helped spread and sustain the AI boom. Jensen Huang's exit had raised doubts about the fragility of this system, and the interim management had suggested a more "disciplined and selective" approach.The concerns about so-called "circular financing" still raise concerns from some analysts. The public backlash against datacentres and AI evident at the US midterm elections also point to a changed environment. The Democrats in Congress have vowed to investigate both the President and Mr Huang, and he is due to appear before them next week. Jensen Huang is at the centre of it all - the technology, the financing, the US politics and the geopolitics.Today has proven Jensen Huang was in fact, too big to fire.

schema.headline: Why Jensen Huang proved too big to fire

title: No 10 North will face greater scrutiny as Andy Burnham's 10-year plan looms
description: The work of Andy Burnham's new Number 10 North office in Manchester has been kept largely away from the headlines since it opened in July.But the offi
body: The work of Andy Burnham's new Number 10 North office in Manchester has been kept largely away from the headlines since it opened in July.But the officials based there are mainly focused on two soon-to-be-published documents that could go on to define his time as prime minister.The first is Burnham's 10-year plan, which is due next month, and which the prime minister says will lay out a path "to where I believe we all want Britain to be".The second is the 'rewiring the state' white paper, a detailed policy document that will follow in the new year and should give the clearest indication yet of what power Burnham hopes to move away from Westminster to other parts of the country.But despite Burnham insisting his new Manchester team will be the "engine room" of change, others in government question how much difference they can really make.There's talk among Labour MPs that the 10-year plan, which has also had significant input from Westminster departments, will not go as far as the prime minister had hoped.But one official who has seen elements of the plan said it will be "pretty weighty" and include "quite a lot of radicalism".Number 10 North has been focused on how the plan can deliver on Burnham's pledge to achieve "growth in every postcode".One major theme is expected to be reindustrialisation, with advisers exploring how to attract businesses to less prosperous towns and cities.Staff in Manchester are also said to be looking at what parts of the country may not see growth through reindustrialisation – such as some rural and coastal areas – and what the alternative offer for those places could be.Eyebrows were raised in Whitehall this summer when a government statement said that "local economic growth policy" would be transferred "from HM Treasury directly into No 10 North".Some saw that as an attempt to disempower the Treasury, but sources there insist that no serious decisions on growth can be made without the department's involvement and approval.When Burnham first announced plans for the Manchester base, he singled out housing as an issue on which it would take the lead.In a speech last month Number 10 North's deputy director highlighted health, transport and education as other areas it was focused on.While it's understood the 10-year plan is likely to include long-term ambitions for social care, skills training and council housebuilding, there are doubts within government departments about exactly how involved Number 10 North will eventually be in those areas.One Whitehall official said "most things" that have been announced as Number 10 North priorities have in practice "stayed with other departments".They said Number 10 North is "not doing delivery" because it "doesn't have its own resource" and is "underpowered compared to departments" in London.A recent hiring spree will see around 120 officials and advisers working from Number 10 North when it moves into its permanent premises next spring.That is almost half of the around 280 staff members that work for "Number 10 South", a term some advisers are now using for Downing Street.But even those staffing levels are only a fraction of the numbers employed by other departments.The Treasury's north of England campus in Darlington, which was set up in 2021, has around 3,000 staff.John Healey is said to have been particularly impressed with the Darlington campus's record of hiring people who would otherwise not have joined the civil service, something Downing Street hopes to achieve in Manchester too.Darlington's most senior civil servant, Beth Russell, has been working with Number 10 North to share her experience of how best to set up a new government office outside London.Prime ministers have for decades been frustrated by how little power Number 10 can sometimes wield within Whitehall, arguing that levers can be pulled but nothing then happens.One question at the heart of the Number 10 North project is whether it will eventually wield genuine power itself or merely decide which powers to take from Westminster and give to mayors and other regional politicians around the country.A government source said Number 10 North's current role is "more in convening" people from elsewhere and argued the prime minister would need to choose what he wanted it to do in the future.They added: "I could see it going two different ways."Will it be more delivery or will it be more in the conventional role of Number 10?"Maybe it's not best placed to do things, but maybe directing and convening are also important things to do."Regional mayors have been regular visitors of Number 10 North and are set to be earmarked for much more expansive powers in the 'rewiring the state' white paper.England currently has 14 metro mayors, a number which is likely to be expanded in the coming years.Sources in both Number 10 and the Treasury say "fiscal devolution" will be a major part of the Burnham agenda.People close to the prime minister say that is likely to ultimately mean more cash-raising, spending and borrowing power for mayors.Two of Burnham's early announcements this summer saw mayors given a share of income tax and the ability to introduce a tourist tax for people visiting their areas.The Treasury believes one of the most underreported elements of Healey's Budget last month was a £1.5bn borrowing facility that will be given to mayors from 2028.Sources say that in the future projects such as Doncaster-Sheffield Airport, which Healey gave his backing to, could be given the financial go-ahead directly by mayors, without the need for a separate thumbs up from the chancellor.For now mayors have each been asked to submit a list of projects to Number 10 North, which they feel are being held up by government processes.Government departments in Westminster have also been asked to identify what areas they are currently responsible for which could potentially be devolved to mayors and other local government officials.What's less clear is how the prime minister's devolution plans will affect Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland and whether he is keen for them too to adopt a mayoral model.At a recent meeting in Glasgow, Burnham said he would discuss that further with the leaders of the devolved nations.He recently rejected a proposal from the First Minister of Wales to devolve more responsibilities over policing and justice.Away from the gaze of backbench MPs, opposition parties and Westminster journalists, Number 10 North has so far been able to go about its business without drawing much attention.But as Burnham's long-term plans for the country start to become more clear, the scrutiny faced by his Manchester power base is likely to grow too.

schema.headline: No 10 North will face greater scrutiny as Andy Burnham's 10-year plan looms

title: Blaina girl Lilly Jones stabbed by 14-year-old boy, murder trial told
description: Warning: This article contains details readers may find distressing A teenage girl was stabbed "around 55 times" by a 14-year-old boy, a murder trial
body: Warning: This article contains details readers may find distressing A teenage girl was stabbed "around 55 times" by a 14-year-old boy, a murder trial has been told.Lilly Jones, from Blaina, in Blaenau Gwent, left home at about 18:30 on 20 June, telling her father she was "popping out for a bit".Her body was discovered face down in woodland close to Duffryn Park two days later.A 14-year-old boy, who cannot be named because he is under 18, denies her murder.He and Lilly shared an interest in Pokémon and were "in some kind of relationship", the court heard.The boy was dressed in a white short-sleeved shirt and tie as he sat in the dock at Newport Crown Court on Monday.Anna Pope KC, prosecuting, told the jury a camping knife containing a complete DNA profile had been found in the boy's bedroom drawer."It was calculated to be a billion times more likely if this DNA had come from Lilly Jones than if it had come from someone else," she said.Pope said the boy had not given an explanation as to why Lilly's DNA was on the knife.She added scratch marks were discovered on the inside of his arm and forensic swabs taken from Lilly's fingernails identified his DNA.She had been stabbed in the heart, both lungs and an artery in her neck. There were 17 stab wounds to her neck, and knife wounds were found on her face, jaw, chest and bottom.Lilly's phone has never been found.Newport Crown Court was told Lilly and the boy became friends in March this year after a chance meeting in the street.They were captured on CCTV cameras in Blaina and were last seen together at 18:50 as they walked towards a footbridge leading to the park, near to where her body was later found.At 22:19 that evening, Lilly's family contacted the police to report her missing. It was the day after her 14th birthday.Police searching for Lilly spoke to the teenager the following day. He told officers he was supposed to meet up with Lilly at the Red Lion pub in Blaina, but she never arrived.He later told police they had been together for part of the previous night, before they separated. He said he came home after she told him she was going to meet up with someone else.In a further conversation with police on the day Lilly's body was found, he said she had told him she wanted to show him a disused park, before leaving.When he was arrested he told police he did not murder Lilly and did not know where her phone was.The trial heard that, when a phone belonging to the defendant was examined, he was found to have searched for Gwent Police, and similar terms, about 30 times the morning after Lilly disappeared, between 05:49 and 10:02.Pope added: "The phone also showed that photographs had been taken by someone using [the defendant's] phone, we say that's [the defendant]."She added it was "of note" that one of the photographs "is looking back towards the scene where we say Lilly's body was later found".Addressing the jury, Pope said: "We will ask you to consider why it is that [the defendant] would take a photograph of some distance, of the area where we know Lilly to have died that night? Particularly if, as he suggests, he left her alive, when she was going to meet a friend."The trial continues.

schema.headline: Blaina girl Lilly Jones stabbed by 14-year-old boy, murder trial told

title: Man City charges: Kevin de Bruyne's feelings will 'never change' even if titles are stripped
description: City await any sanctions that may be imposed following their guilty verdict, with possible punishments ranging from a hefty fine, points deductions, r
body: City await any sanctions that may be imposed following their guilty verdict, with possible punishments ranging from a hefty fine, points deductions, relegation from the Premier League and being stripped of titles.Asserting its innocence, City said it had filed "a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence [that] exists in support of all of its positions" on 2 October.Sources have told BBC Sport that City were expected to claim that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners, as part of an appeal.Criticism of City has been intense, but De Bruyne said he can't "change anything" about people calling his former club a "disgrace"."Of course, in life there are rules, but everybody plays on the limit, I would say, and for me, I played in between the white lines," he said."I don't think a lot of people will change in their mind how they view me as a player, or how we played, but everybody has their own opinion."De Bruyne will be afforded a generous ovation when he returns to Etihad Stadium, having played more than 400 games for City, scoring 108 goals.After his final home game for the club in May 2025, it was announced that a statue will be built in his honour outside the stadium.

schema.headline: Man City charges: Kevin de Bruyne's feelings will 'never change' even if titles are stripped

title: Timms report to suggest faster Pip payments for some disabled people
description: A review into the main disability benefit is set to recommend that those with the most severe conditions and terminal illnesses should get quicker pay
body: A review into the main disability benefit is set to recommend that those with the most severe conditions and terminal illnesses should get quicker payments.The report on Personal Independence Payment (Pip), which will be published on Tuesday afternoon, will also suggest that assessments are overhauled to provide claimants in England and Wales with more appropriate support.But despite the cost of the benefit projected to more than double between 2020 and 2030, the review is understood not to suggest major savings.Groups representing disabled people - who had a hand in drafting the report - have broadly welcomed its findings.The review, chaired by the Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms, was asked by the government to explore how the benefit, claimed by around four million people, could be made "fair and fit for the future in a changing world".The review was set up last year after the Starmer government's aborted attempt to cut welfare spending.Sir Stephen set out several proposals in an article in the Times on Monday, which are likely to be accepted by ministers.These include that disability benefit payments should be linked to real-life needs and the extra costs incurred by the claimant, rather than their diagnosis.As part of that, those with the most severe and persistent conditions would be fast-tracked with no further assessments involved - believed to be the case for about one in 10 claimants. The aim, wrote Sir Stephen, was to create a process that was "less burdensome".The government is set to spend £32.1bn on Pip this financial year, a figure that is projected to rise to £41.5bn in 2030-31. In 2019-20, the year before the pandemic, Pip cost £16.3bn, when adjusted for inflation to today's prices."Disability claims have risen fastest amongst young people who are the least likely to be become seriously ill as a result of the pandemic," said Matt Ryder, a policy consultant with the free-market think tank the Adam Smith Institute."We need to target lower-level mental health claims. That seems to be the root cause of the rising claims, so we need to restrict eligibility for that."Research last month from the Resolution Foundation, a think tank focused on lower and middle earners, suggested about one in six Pip recipients said they didn't incur any extra costs due to their disability.The think tank suggests removing Pip from this group would save up to £4.4m a year.Lindsay Judge, research director at the Resolution Foundation, said although the Timms Review did not set out to cut costs, "they should be possible nonetheless"."The Timms Review rightly stated this summer that the current system of Pip is not fit for purpose, and that major change is needed."In its final report, the review must set out clearly how the system can work better. This should include assessments that seek to better understand disabled people's needs; awards - either through cash or services - that better reflect the actual costs that disabled people face; and more regular light touch check-ins so that changes of circumstances are fully understood."Ryder said fewer reassessments for people with deteriorating conditions, and making the process more accessible were "individually the right thing for disabled people" but that the think tank were concerned abut the rising costs of Pip."The cost at the moment is acceptable, but it's where the cost is heading. The number of claimants has roughly doubled since before the pandemic. According to the OBR, we can expect that spending on Pip will rise to £47bn in five years' time. And there's no reason why it would stop at that point. Why wouldn't it continue on growing?"The proposals will be put forward by a steering group, led by Sir Stephen, which the government will respond to.There were concerns from disability charities that Pip payments might become means-tested or the cash payments partially replaced with vouchers, but it is understood this will not be the case.James Taylor, head of strategy at disability charity Scope, said the organisation agreed Pip assessments needed an overhaul."Disabled people have told us the process is stressful and degrading. Fast-tracking claims and ending unnecessary reassessments for people with severe conditions could make a real difference."A better assessment should recognise the extra costs disabled people face, and should include what they need and what they are already going without. If you can't afford the taxi you need because public transport is inaccessible, the cost hasn't gone away. People need reliable cash support they can use as their needs change, whether they're in work or out of work."Alicia Cartwright in Preston receives the higher rate of Pip for both the daily living and mobility components, which she says equates to about £500 every four weeks.Cartwright is a power wheelchair user and works several part-time jobs at a university.She says the costs of her disabilities run to a further £1,500 a month which she has to pay out of her wages."The mobility part of it, that goes on paying for my wheelchair. And then the rest of my Pip goes entirely on paying someone to help me around the house"The mum of two is a trained benefits advisor, but says even she finds the current assessment process "intimidating and confusing"."Trust disabled people to know what their needs are. Of course, have some checks in there, absolutely, but we really need to start from a place of trust."Currently, in any dealings with the benefits system, you feel like you're on trial, and for a lot of people, asking for help is difficult in the first place."The disability benefit system is devolved in Scotland and will not change in line with England and Wales, but the Timms Review could impact the funding the Scottish government receives.Disability benefits are also devolved in Northern Ireland, but in practice it reflects any changes made to the system in England and Wales.

schema.headline: Timms report to suggest faster Pip payments for some disabled people

title: Comedian impersonates Trump's dance moves, mocks trade talks at Canada press dinner
description: Prime Minister Mark Carney brought a Donald Trump impersonator on stage at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner, where he poked fun at strained US-Can
body: Prime Minister Mark Carney brought a Donald Trump impersonator on stage at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner, where he poked fun at strained US-Canada relations and on-again, off-again trade talks.The impersonator, played by comedian Mark Critch of the sketch comedy show This Hour Has 22 Minutes, came out after Carney jokingly pressed an "emergency comedy button" during his speech.Critch appeared alongside another actor impersonating Carney, played by Canadian sketch comedian Mark McKinney. "We've got two Carneys here, it's a disaster," the Trump impersonator said after he walked on stage.Using some of Trump's signature mannerisms, like his dance moves and his slightly hunched posture, he joked about the latest US midterm elections, which led to Trump's Republican Party losing control in Congress. "I'm so popular we just had a big BLUE WAVE in the states," the impersonator said at the Saturday press gala. He also took aim at ongoing US-Canada trade negotiations, saying,"We're going to have a great deal. There's only one thing standing in the way: me, because I'm crazy."There were also jabs at Trump's search for a new White House press secretary following Katie Zacharia's exit, and at US ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra, who is unpopular among Canadians."I said 'find somebody who is less likeable than me,' and we got one," the Trump impersonator joked about Hoekstra.Carney stood behind him occasionally laughing. The prime minister also delivered his own zingers, saying at one point: "This is a tough room. And I've been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator."Both Critch and McKinney - the two impersonators - are fixtures of This Hour Has 22 Minutes, a long-standing Canadian sketch comedy show that has recently enjoyed viral internet fame for its timely skits mocking the Trump administration. The skits, published directly on Tik Tok and YouTube, have depicted Zacharia's quick ouster, external and poked fun at rapper Nicki Minaj's, external support for Trump. They have garnered millions of views, and even captured the attention of major US media., externalCritch and McKinney's appearance at Saturday's dinner is part of an evening of traditionally light-hearted humour, where Canadian politicians poke fun at one another at a gala hosted by the Canadian Parliamentary Press Gallery.In a separate speech, Canada's governor general, Louise Arbour, joked about Carney's popularity and frequent global travel."Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he's supposed to be," Arbour said.

schema.headline: Comedian impersonates Trump's dance moves, mocks trade talks at Canada press dinner

title: Analysis: Can Andy Burnham turn volume down on UK rejoining EU debate?
description: When the prime minister told MPs "there will be no banging on about Europe" from him, my mind flashed back 20 years.It is 2006 and a fresh faced David
body: When the prime minister told MPs "there will be no banging on about Europe" from him, my mind flashed back 20 years.It is 2006 and a fresh faced David Cameron had just taken over as the Conservative leader, promising, yes you guessed it, to stop "banging on" about Europe. And we all know how that turned out: a decade later as prime minister, he held and lost a referendum on whether the UK should stay in the European Union, as he advocated, or leave.Andy Burnham's address to the Commons, after Friday's EU-UK Summit in Brussels, felt like an attempt by a man who chose to turn the Europe conversation up to full blast this autumn, to try to turn the volume back down again.All of this prompts two big questions: whether he will be able to do that and what, in the end, Labour promises at the next general election.Asked if that could include seeking a mandate for another in/out referendum at that election, he didn't rule that out."If it's in Britain's national interest, I will recommend it to this House. If it is not, then I won't," he said.But he very carefully left his options open: "There is no fixed opinion here. There is no fixed destination."So he might offer a referendum. Or he might not.He also suggested the frequency of his public utterances on the subject may be limited, insisting there would be no "running commentary," offering instead what he called "a calm, constructive and pragmatic consideration of what is in Britain's interest in the long term."Plus, he said Europe could change in the coming years. A nod, without naming her, that Marine Le Pen could become president of France, for instance. How might that shift the debate?Burnham's willingness to repeatedly talk about the European question in the last few months has, inevitably, spawned quite the reaction.A campaign group, Stay Out, has got itself up and running to argue exactly that.And the European Movement is helping launch a rival outfit called, again, you guessed it, Get In.It is a reminder that that the EU question has a knack of getting under the skin of British politics, often to the exclusion of other things, sometimes to the exclusion of seemingly everything.Can the prime minister successfully manage the volume switch so the topic is background hubbub in 2027, rather than a deafening din?Meanwhile, what does the European Union itself make of all of this? EU sources see Andy Burnham's desire to "brainstorm" with them what the future relationship might look like as "normal diplomacy" as one figure put it, adding: "I don't think there are many options. And they are clear. The status quo. The customs union. The single market. And full membership."They mirror his expectation that "brainstorming" won't involve additional meetings, let alone a structured set of bespoke talks arriving at a conclusion. "We don't need a template. It will be part of the regular discussion," is how it was put to me.On Thursday, the government will publish its European Partnerships Bill, the legislation needed to enact, at the UK end, the agreements reached at the summit. Also later this week, the legal text of those agreements is due to be published – the small print of which will be pored over.How much might the UK have to compensate the EU for, for instance, if a future government were to decide to reverse the changes that have just been signed up to? Within the deal it is expected that were Britain to change its mind on the food export part of the deal in the next 10 years, Brussels would charge London for the reinstallation of the checkpoints that will soon no longer be needed.Then, there are the ongoing negotiations between the two sides about unresolved areas of potential cooperation. The EU has made much of its desire to secure a deal on university tuition fees in the next six months, with the hope that EU students will pay no more at UK universities than British students do. The deal would be reciprocal for UK students studying elsewhere in Europe. Both sides think an agreement is within reach. Senior figures in Whitehall are also encouraged by the EU's willingness to include the UK in its 'Made in Europe' plan to protect European industry from China. Then there is the EU's common electricity market.But even if all these things are agreed – and they will all provoke debate here about whether or not they are good ideas – Andy Burnham has publicly said incremental changes only take the UK so far.It is clear he has an appetite and an interest in going further. The question, ultimately, is how much further?

schema.headline: Analysis: Can Andy Burnham turn volume down on UK rejoining EU debate?

title: Why I don't always tell potential employers I'm dyslexic
description: Nineteen-year-old Ayana Bailey doesn't always disclose her dyslexia in job applications, in case it counts against her."It's not like there's going to
body: Nineteen-year-old Ayana Bailey doesn't always disclose her dyslexia in job applications, in case it counts against her."It's not like there's going to be a target on my back, but I'm just like, 'maybe they won't select me'," says Bailey, a part-time florist.A British Dyslexia Association (BDA) survey of more than 1,200 working dyslexic adults found Bailey isn't alone - with 46% hiding their dyslexia at work.Some 81% believe the condition adds to their work-related stress.Bailey was diagnosed aged 11 and says she received good support at school, including mentoring, which helped her to understand her strengths and manage low self-esteem.But the world of work has proved more challenging.For Bailey, the application process is "daunting". She says she relies on her mum to go through it with her.In interviews, Bailey says: "I just shut down. I completely forget who I am."One way of coping, she says, is to have a little script, but she admits it doesn't always work.Bailey, who studied film and wants to go into the creative arts, says that while dyslexia has sometimes made her feel anxious, it's also given her opportunities."I would definitely say my creativity and thinking outside the box [is my biggest strength]."She says her dyslexia makes her a visual learner - able to imagine characters before seeing any written descriptions and helping her dream of becoming a casting director.

schema.headline: Why I don't always tell potential employers I'm dyslexic

title: Women's World Cup 2035: UK host bid is confirmed by Fifa
description: England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales will jointly host the 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa has confirmed.It will be the first time a football Wo
body: England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales will jointly host the 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa has confirmed.It will be the first time a football World Cup has been held in the United Kingdom since the men's tournament in 1966.The four countries were the only bidders for the tournament, and were ratified as co-hosts at a specially arranged virtual meeting from Fifa's Zurich headquarters.The tournament will consist of 104 matches contested by 48 teams over 39 days.The 'All Together' bid included a proposal to use 19 venues, with 14 in England, one in Northern Ireland, two in Scotland and two in Wales.Monday's special meeting of Fifa's Congress also approved the joint bid by Mexico, the United States, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031 finals, which will be the first to feature 48 teams.The news comes on the same day the UK government announced a vision for one million more girls to play, watch or be in leadership roles in sport by the time the tournament takes place. England failed to win the right to host the men's World Cups in 2006 and 2018, and a proposed UK and Ireland bid for the 2030 tournament was abandoned.But England and Scotland hosted matches at the men's Euros in 2021, and England staged the women's European Championship in 2022, which the Lionesses won.England, Scotland, Wales, and the Republic of Ireland will jointly host the men's European Championship in 2028.Mark Bullingham, chief executive of the Football Association, said: "Hosting Euro 2022 allowed us to change the game in our country, by creating a generation of aspirational role models and growing demand from women and girls to play."Hosting a World Cup would give us the chance to build on that across all four nations."The English stadiums included in the 2035 bid are: Villa Park, The Amex, Ashton Gate, Elland Road, Hill Dickinson Stadium, Emirates Stadium, Selhurst Park, Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Wembley, Etihad Stadium, St James' Park, the City Ground, the Stadium of Light and Old Trafford.If Manchester United's proposed new Old Trafford stadium does not go ahead, it would still be considered in its current form.Cardiff City Stadium and Principality Stadium are the two Welsh venues, with Easter Road in Edinburgh and Hampden Park in Glasgow in Scotland.Northern Ireland missed out on co-hosting the men's Euros in 2028 after the UK government said in 2024 it would not provide funding to redevelop Casement Park in time - but a redeveloped Windsor Park is set to stage matches in 2035.A further three stadiums could be added - Birmingham's new Powerhouse Stadium, Wrexham's redeveloped Racecourse Ground, and a potential new Chelsea ground - which would take the tournament to 16 cities and 22 venues.Fifa is yet to decide whether all four co-hosts will qualify automatically.The participation of women and girls in football has risen by 2.3m since the Women's European Championship was held in England in 2022.However, women remain significantly underrepresented in leadership positions. Only a quarter of chief executive, chair or performance director roles in major UK sports are held by women and only 12% of sports federations are led by a female.Noel Mooney, the chief executive of the Football Association of Wales, said: "This is a proud day for Welsh football."We've put forward Wrexham and Cardiff as host cities, and it's exciting to think what a World Cup could bring to both cities and the communities around them."In Llunio Cymru - our 10-year strategy - we've set ourselves the ambition of reaching the knockout stages in 2035. Some of the players who could take us there are learning the game at clubs across Wales today. Our job is to make sure that wherever a girl grows up in Wales, she can find a team close to home, have a coach who helps her develop and see a route to the Cymru shirt."Irish Football Association chief executive Patrick Nelson said the event "would be felt in every club and every age group, in every part of the country"."Our young players would grow up having watched the best in the world play at home, and there is no substitute for that," he added.Scottish Football Association chief executive Ian Maxwell said hosting the tournament would be "the most significant thing to happen to the women's and girls' game in Scotland".He added: "The impact would go far beyond just the matches themselves. The level of investment into coaching, facilities and player pathways in the years beforehand will shape the future of the game for the generations to come."Fifa's evaluation, published earlier this month, rated the bid 4.3 out of five. Its contractual framework was rated 'medium risk', and the document claimed "certain government guarantees contain material qualifications, particularly regarding tax and safety and security".That is thought to refer to a lack of agreement over a request by Fifa for tax-free status for all football-related activities.The bid evaluation said: "The bidder has submitted an extensive set of government support documents and contractual hosting agreements, demonstrating the commitment of the relevant authorities and stakeholders."However, certain government guarantees, particularly those relating to safety and security and tax, contain certain qualifications which have been duly noted in the legal evaluation."While certain contractual matters remain subject to further discussion, the bidder's proactive engagement with Fifa and the substantial lead-in time provide a sound basis for resolving these outstanding issues."

schema.headline: Women's World Cup 2035: UK host bid is confirmed by Fifa

title: Missile on truck in Llangollen goes viral on TikTok
description: A 20ft-long Cold War era missile perched on the back of a truck in a field has become a hit on TikTok - and revealed a love story behind it.Photos and
body: A 20ft-long Cold War era missile perched on the back of a truck in a field has become a hit on TikTok - and revealed a love story behind it.Photos and videos of the striking sight near Llangollen, Denbighshire, spread across social media, prompting speculation, theories and curious comments from people wondering how it got there and why.But for the man who owns it, the story has nothing to do with secret military operations or preparations for war - it is about him using an unusual hobby to honour his late wife.Adrian Hyde, 59, admits it has now "all just snowballed and I've got carried away" and has spent about £200,000 on numerous vehicles.Military enthusiasts Adrian and his wife Janette spent years talking about owning a military vehicle and planned to buy a tank as a joint 50th birthday present."We had all the area and ground ready, the driveway ready. We knew exactly where we were going to buy it from. We were going to buy a Russian one from Poland," said Adrian.But this dream was put on hold when Janette was diagnosed with cancer in 2016.Despite having cancer three times, Adrian said she never lost her determination and the couple "kept saying 'we'll eventually get that tank'. I think that's what kept us going".Janette died in January 2025 at the age of 57, and Adrian found himself returning to their shared dream and bought the tank three months later.The unusual sight quickly attracted attention locally before exploding online after a video posted, external by a hiker and content creator went "absolutely viral" on TikTok and Instagram.Adrian said: "I've had people ringing me about it. I've got loads of people trying to get friendly on Facebook. It's gone crazy."To me it's natural, I have always grown up with military kit, but I suppose it is different."He said many people have commented saying the missile was live, but that was "ludicrous"."It's all inactive. It's from the 1950s but in mint condition," he said.The Thunderbird was withdrawn from service in the 1980s, according to the Imperial War Museum."The missile is a Thunderbird missile from the Cold War era, but everything has been stripped off it."The inside is hollow. It's got the original outside shell but the inside all the electronics, explosives, jets, they've all been taken off and decommissioned."A friend made the frame for it and bolted it on the back of a 1957 Bedford truck.While many may see his military collection as odd, Adrian said it represented a dream he and Janette talked about for years, but never had the chance to realise together."It's quite emotional because it was our dream for 10 years. Janette would have loved it."But the military equipment is not the only way Adrian has honoured his wife.

schema.headline: Missile on truck in Llangollen goes viral on TikTok

title: Tarkowski's first Premier League red ruins Moyes' night - was it deserved?
description: So what exactly happened?Just 15 minutes after Keane Lewis-Potter scored his second deflected strike of the evening, Everton skipper Tarkowski thunder
body: So what exactly happened?Just 15 minutes after Keane Lewis-Potter scored his second deflected strike of the evening, Everton skipper Tarkowski thundered into a challenge on Brentford's Yehor Yarmoliuk.He won the ball but also followed through with the challenge forcefully. Initially, referee Craig Pawson deemed a foul and a yellow card was enough.But, after an intervention from the video assistant referee (VAR) and studying the replay, Pawson changed the yellow for a red.The Premier League match centre said on X: "After VAR review, the referee overturned the original decision of yellow card for Tarkowski for the challenge on Yarmoliuk and issued a red card for serious foul play. "VAR: 'Point of contact is on the shin. He's got speed and intensity. Studs are high.'"REF: 'After review, Everton No.6 commits a challenge that endangers his opponent's safety, making contact with the studs onto the shin. Cancelling the yellow card - and a red card.'"Referees are asked to take into account several considerations for what counts as serious foul play including the speed of the challenge, its intensity, force and what degree of control there was.But, as always, there was plenty of debate about whether it was the correct decision.BBC Sport's football issues correspondent Dale Johnson, said: "Really not sure about this as a VAR red card. "Yes, Tarkowski absolutely ticks the boxes for speed and intensity and leading high with studs showing. "But the question marks are that Tarkowski made only small contact and didn't have a straight leg when he did so."Maybe his reputation played a part? Remember, he wrongly escaped a VAR red card against Liverpool for a challenge, which was along the same lines. He won the ball and then followed through into Alexis Mac Allister. Thought that was a far stronger challenge."BBC Radio 5 Live's - and former Blackburn Rovers striker - Chris Sutton, said on X: "Come on that's not a red… the game's gone."Former Arsenal striker Alan Smith agreed the decision was harsh. He told Sky Sports: "Ten years ago we wouldn't have looked at it once and now we still [frame] it on the follow-through. I just can't see it."Only Tarkowski knows if he wanted to leave it high or if it was natural. The follow-through was just natural momentum."There's a bit of anger in there from Tarkowski and it's a little high but only he knows if he wanted to leave a little more on Yarmoliuk there."Opinion was far from unanimous though, with both pundits in the Sky Sports studio adamant it was a clear red.Former Liverpool centre-back Jamie Carragher said: "It's a red card. Tarkowski has got previous for tackles like that. He is a 90s defender, he tackles like that."He follows through with such force, it is excessive. You want to give him the benefit of the doubt but it's a red card."He added: "You could argue was it a big enough mistake for VAR to get involved but I think we are splitting hairs. He doesn't need to do this."While ex-Totenham defender Toby Alderweireld added: "It's a red card, he knows what he is doing. 100%."Josh, Sheffield: Never a red for Tarkowski and I'm a Liverpool fan. What's he meant to do? Stop momentum. It's a good tackle and the player runs into the natural follow throughRobin, Essex: Another game ruined by VAR! Not straight leg tackle you can surely see he turned his foot around. Poor!Rob, Manchester: These sorts of VAR decisions are making me turn off football. Why pay all that money to watch arbitrary decisions impact the game? Lee: It is a sad day when a good tackle gets a player sent off. You slow anything down and dissect it you can find wrongs. Yellow was a bit much and the red ridiculous, we need ex players in the VAR decisions too.Max, Oldham: What a load of nonsense the red card is. Tarkowski can't stop his momentum. VAR has ruined another game, plus what is the ref doing? He had a chance to stick with the yellow card. Another case of an official who has never played the game. Paul, St Asaph: Tarkowski has got away with that same foul a few times. Do think he's the type of player to leave one in on purpose.Anon: Yes it's a red - Tarkowski knows what he's doing, it's frustration and wanting to leave a bit on the player.Chris, Chelmsford: He does it all the time at the borderline but about time he got one. Woody, London: Lack of refinement masked as passion, classic Tarkowski tackle there… glad to see him off.George, Birmingham: Studs up in a tackle, he has to go. A clear red card for me.

schema.headline: Tarkowski's first Premier League red ruins Moyes' night - was it deserved?

title: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports
description: Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after reports that Russia was preparing to launch a nuclear-armed
body: Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after reports that Russia was preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media outlets. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.Asked about the reports, Rutte said: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element."Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hadn't seen the latest reports but dismissed reports citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".Rutte told the press conference in Berlin that Nato had a variety of response options."When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary," he said.Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, the reports by broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites. Standing alongside Rutte, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue"."Reports that Russia is planning to introduce nuclear weaponry into space are not new, yet they remain no less shocking," he said.A German government spokesman earlier also did not confirm or deny the reports, but said it was taking the reports "very seriously", AFP reported. The spokesman, however, warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, said having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario", German paper Handelsblatt reported.Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit. Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.In 2024 the US claimed Russia was developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation. "Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time.In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".

schema.headline: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports

title: Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say
description: A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities
body: A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom."We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said."The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari."Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.

schema.headline: Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say

title: Don Toliver postpones London O2 arena show after Manchester evacuation
description: US rapper Don Toliver has postponed two shows in London this week, after his concert in Manchester on Sunday was evacuated when an "unknown substance"
body: US rapper Don Toliver has postponed two shows in London this week, after his concert in Manchester on Sunday was evacuated when an "unknown substance" was released into the crowd. Toliver was due to play The O2 on Monday and Wembley Arena on Tuesday, but  Live Nation said his "stage and production equipment remains in Manchester and cannot be moved in time".One person was taken to hospital and 89 people showed "symptoms believed to be linked to the exposure" after Sunday's Co-op Live arena show, police said.Fans described "distressing scenes" with people "choking", "screaming" and "coughing up blood" because of the effects of a substance, which police initially believed to be tear gas.The Wembley show has been rescheduled to 14 December, while Monday night's O2 gig has been moved to 15 December."I'm very sad to sit here and say I have to reschedule The O2 London show to December 15th due to (the) unfortunate incident last night," Don Toliver wrote on Instagram. Greater Manchester Police (GMP) declared a major incident on Sunday and said 12,000 people were evacuated from the arena.One woman was taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment and treatment after the incident, which happened at about 22:00 GMT, the force said.A further 88 people "underwent dry decontamination at the scene and were subsequently accommodated within the Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed", according to GMP.Leon Douzi said he was right next to where the substance was released, and described someone holding a can and "this gas coming out"."It just hit me in the throat," he said, adding that it felt like "burning".There was "a bit of panic", Douzi said: "Everybody was having the same feeling and trying to get out."Some fans reported eye and respiratory symptoms, according to the North West Ambulance Service.Hannah Baxter, who went to the concert with her partner, said the first thing she noticed was a burning feeling in her throat."[We] were just coughing and coughing... there was a guy next to us who had vomited. There were people with red eyes and... tears everywhere," she told the BBC.Joey Howe, a football journalist at the gig, told BBC Radio Manchester there was a "horrible smell" and added: "People were coming through in wheelchairs choking – it was really distressing."Police launched an investigation and are continuing to carry out tests on items at the venue to try to identify the substance. No arrests have been made.Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said: "Enquiries remain ongoing to establish the nature of the substance, where it came from and any associated risk. Testing will take place throughout the day as the investigation into the cause of this incident progresses."We are trying to establish whether any criminality has occurred in relation to this incident."Some fans complained about security and a lack of searches as people went into the Manchester concert.Jessica Moult-Boffey, of Wigan, said people were "crying and screaming in pain" as they left the venue, adding she felt "confused on how something like that got into a venue of that size".Malachi Clarke also claimed security was "not good at all", adding: "They weren't checking bags, to the point where I had to ask them if they needed to check mine."Co-op Live said on its website there were a range of security measures, and while "some of these are visible, others you won't be able to see".It said the arena used a "frictionless security screening that detects prohibited items without you needing to empty your pockets".Figen Murray, the mother of a Manchester Arena attack victim who led the campaign for a new law to prevent terrorist attacks at public venues, said people should feel "assured" about security measures. "A lot of the big venues use mass screening technology, where you don't even know you've been checked," she told the BBC. They also have staff observing CCTV, security guards and plain-clothed officers on site.Murray said that while the current technology is "good enough", it needed improvement over the next few years to become "more sophisticated".Venues are currently focused on keeping out items – such as explosives – that could cause mass casualties, she added.All fans at the Manchester show will get a full refund, promoter Live Nation said.A statement said: "We are sorry to everyone affected by last night's events in Manchester and full refunds for that show will be automatically processed to ticket holders."There have apparently been similar incidents earlier on Toliver's tour, when some fans reported spray or gas being released into the crowd in Zurich and Paris.In his post on Monday, the rapper said: "I just wanna make sure everyone is safe and the next show goes on properly. My heart and prayers are with everyone that was injured last night.""The only thing I love more than creating music is performing for my fans," Toliver said, asking people to stop bringing substances into his shows."It ain't cool," added the rapper, who was nominated for five Grammy Awards earlier this month. "See you soon London, love you Guys. DT."Toliver's Nitrous tour, named after his new album, is also due to visit Wembley Arena in London on Tuesday. No update has been given about that show.It was set to be the last gig of his world tour before he took a break from the road ahead of a Coachella appearance next spring.Toliver is best known for singles such as No Idea and After Party, from his debut studio album, Heaven or Hell (2020), which was big on TikTok. He also featured on  Travis Scott's song Can't Say, from his third studio album Astroworld.

schema.headline: Don Toliver postpones London O2 arena show after Manchester evacuation
